title: Animals in God's Care
lead: The Bible's God makes the animals and calls them good, makes a covenant with them, feeds them and keeps count of the sparrows. Israel's law gives work animals a Sabbath rest, God's speeches to Job parade the wild creatures no human controls, and the book of Jonah ends with God's pity for Nineveh's people "and many animals too" (Jonah 4:11).

sections.h: Made, blessed and included in the covenant
sections.b:
God made the sea creatures, the birds and the land animals, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:21; Genesis 1:25), before humans were made. Humans are told to rule over them (Genesis 1:28), and the first man names them (Genesis 2:19). After the Flood God makes his covenant not only with Noah's family but "with every living creature that is with you" (Genesis 9:10), and Hosea foresees a covenant "with the wild animals, with the birds of the sky" (Hosea 2:18). The psalmist says, "Humans and animals alike you keep safe, LORD" (Psalm 36:6).

The same Bible lets people use animals. After the Flood God gives them to Noah for food: "Everything that creeps and lives is yours for food" (Genesis 9:3). Israel's law sorts animals into clean and unclean (Leviticus 11) and commands animal sacrifices (Leviticus 1). So the Bible's care for animals is not a ban on killing them. It sets that use inside God's ownership of every creature. See the pages on food laws and on sacrifice.

sections.h: God feeds them: Job 38–41 and Psalm 104
sections.b: When God answers Job, he does not explain Job's suffering; he shows him the animals. The lion and the raven, the ibex, the wild donkey, the wild ox, the ostrich, the horse and the hawk pass by (Job 38:39–39:30), then Behemoth and Leviathan (Job 40–41). Almost none of them serve humans; God cares for them anyway, in places no one sees. Psalm 104 sings the same care: grass for the herds, and lions that "ask God for their food" (Psalm 104:21); "They all wait on you / to hand them their food in its season" (Psalm 104:27). Jesus argues from this care: "your heavenly Father feeds them" (Matthew 6:26), and of the sparrows, "not one of them falls to the ground without your Father" (Matthew 10:29), "in God's sight not one of them is forgotten" (Luke 12:6). His point is that people matter more, but it rests on God's real care for the birds.

Israel's law protects animals. The Sabbath is "so that your ox and your donkey can rest" (Exodus 23:12; Deuteronomy 5:14). A traveler may take eggs or young birds from a nest but must let the mother go (Deuteronomy 22:6–7). "Do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing" (Deuteronomy 25:4). Proverbs says, "A righteous man knows what his animal needs" (Proverbs 12:10). The Talmud asks whether the duty to spare animals pain, tza'ar ba'alei chayim, "the suffering of living creatures," comes from the Torah itself (Bavli Bava Metzia 32b). It tests proofs on both sides. It ties the view that the duty is not from the Torah to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, against the other sages, and it keeps returning to the view, which it gives to Rava, that the duty is Torah law. Paul quotes the ox law and asks, "Is it oxen that God cares about?" (1 Corinthians 9:9). He applies it to paying those who preach: "Yes, it was written for our sake" (1 Corinthians 9:10). Readers differ on how far Paul means this. John Calvin held that Paul does not take oxen out of God's care, since God does not overlook even a sparrow. He read Paul to mean that the law had people chiefly in view, and he scorned readers who turn such laws into allegories (Commentary on 1 Corinthians, on 9:9). In Nineveh even the animals fast and wear sackcloth (Jonah 3:7–8), and God's last word to Jonah counts them among those he pities (Jonah 4:11).

sections.b: Isaiah pictures a day when "The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb" (Isaiah 11:6) and nothing will hurt on God's holy mountain. Readers take this in more than one way. John Calvin read it chiefly of people: those who were like wolves and bears become gentle under Christ. Yet he also saw in it a restored world, where animals no longer prey on each other (Commentary on Isaiah, on 11:6). Paul says "the creation itself will also be set free from slavery to decay" (Romans 8:21). Calvin took "creation" there to mean all creatures, animals included, but he warned that it is not right to ask too curiously what that will mean for the beasts (Commentary on Romans, on 8:21). John Wesley, preaching on Romans 8:19–22, went further. He held that animals "shall one day be delivered from this bondage of corruption, and shall then receive an ample amends for all their present sufferings" (Sermon 60, "The General Deliverance"). Ecclesiastes leaves the question open: "Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above, and whether the spirit of animals goes down below to the earth?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). Thomas Aquinas taught that an animal's soul, unlike a human soul, does not exist on its own apart from the body, so it does not live on after death (Summa Theologiae I, question 75, articles 3 and 6). Either way, the Bible is plain that animals belong to God, and Proverbs counts care for them as part of being righteous (Proverbs 12:10).
